claim: C. elegans has 302 neurons.
source: The connectome structure among 302 neurons and 165 somatic cells of C. elegans was discovered by pioneering works (Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cook et al., 2019 and White et al., 1986

claim: C. elegans has 165 somatic cells.
source: The connectome structure among 302 neurons and 165 somatic cells of C. elegans was discovered by pioneering works (Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cook et al., 2019 and White et al., 1986

claim: C. elegans matures in about three days.
source: The organism matures in a shorter period, about three days, compared to other model animals such as fruit flies or mice.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about C. elegans development

claim: C. elegans has a transparent body that allows for easy microscopic observation of internal structures.
source: Its transparent body allows for easy microscopic observation of its internal structures or artificially expressed green fluorescent proteins.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about C. elegans physical properties

claim: C. elegans is hermaphroditic.
source: Moreover, due to the hermaphroditic nature of C. elegans, offspring mostly share the same genotype as the parent, which simplifies the multiplication of the worm population for research purposes (Hall and Altun, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hall and Altun, 2008

claim: C. elegans bends its body with a sinusoidal wave pattern when moving forward or backward.
source: C. elegans bends its body with a sinusoidal wave pattern when moving forward or backward.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and supported by citations in the following sentence

claim: The driving force for C. elegans movement comes from the difference between perpendicular and parallel frictional forces.
source: The driving force for this movement comes from the difference between perpendicular and parallel frictional forces, which it experienced from a surrounding environment. This thrust force pushes the worm along the ground surface with which the worm contacts (Berri et al., 2009; Boyle et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2009; Niebur and Erdös, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berri et al., 2009; Boyle et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2009; Niebur and Erdös, 1991

claim: Mature hermaphrodite C. elegans has four muscle strands at the left dorsal, right dorsal, left ventral, and right ventral part of the body.
source: Mature hermaphrodite C. elegans has four muscle strands at the left dorsal, right dorsal, left ventral, and right ventral part of the body, and each muscle strand has 24, 24, 23, and 24 muscle cells, respectively (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986

claim: The left dorsal muscle strand has 24 muscle cells.
source: Mature hermaphrodite C. elegans has four muscle strands at the left dorsal, right dorsal, left ventral, and right ventral part of the body, and each muscle strand has 24, 24, 23, and 24 muscle cells, respectively (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986

claim: The right dorsal muscle strand has 24 muscle cells.
source: Mature hermaphrodite C. elegans has four muscle strands at the left dorsal, right dorsal, left ventral, and right ventral part of the body, and each muscle strand has 24, 24, 23, and 24 muscle cells, respectively (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986

claim: The left ventral muscle strand has 23 muscle cells.
source: Mature hermaphrodite C. elegans has four muscle strands at the left dorsal, right dorsal, left ventral, and right ventral part of the body, and each muscle strand has 24, 24, 23, and 24 muscle cells, respectively (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986

claim: The right ventral muscle strand has 24 muscle cells.
source: Mature hermaphrodite C. elegans has four muscle strands at the left dorsal, right dorsal, left ventral, and right ventral part of the body, and each muscle strand has 24, 24, 23, and 24 muscle cells, respectively (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986

claim: The actuator was modeled as a damped torsional spring due to the viscoelastic characteristics of muscle.
source: The actuator was modeled as a damped torsional spring due to the viscoelastic characteristics of muscle (Boyle et al., 2012; Hill, 1938).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boyle et al., 2012 and Hill, 1938

claim: The average velocity of the worm during crawling is 0.208 mm/s.
source: The average velocity of the worm is 0.208 (mm/s), which is consistent with the known values (Cohen et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2016; Omura et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: Calculated from simulation and consistent with cited experimental values

claim: The average velocity of the worm during swimming is 0.223 mm/s.
source: Thus, the speed of the worm exhibited significant oscillations over time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and the average velocity was 0.223 (mm/s).
evidence: Calculated from simulation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: During crawling, the body part placed diagonally with respect to the direction of the worm's locomotion is pushing along the ground surface.
source: Indeed, we found that the body part placed diagonally with respect to the direction of the worm's locomotion is pushing along the ground surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Found from simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: During swimming, the worm gained significant momentum in the forward direction when the body bent in the c-shape.
source: The worm gained significant momentum in the forward direction of locomotion when the body bent in the c-shape (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Found from simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: During swimming, the speed of the worm exhibited significant oscillations over time.
source: In contrast to crawling, during swimming, the worm did not receive constant thrust force over time. Thus, the speed of the worm exhibited significant oscillations over time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and the average velocity was 0.223 (mm/s).
evidence: Found from simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: During escaping behavior, the worm produced an average power of 2094 fW in the initial forward locomotion.
source: During escaping behavior, the worm produced an average power of 2094 fW in the initial forward locomotion, followed by an average of 16,437 fW (7.85 times that of the initial forward locomotion) in backward locomotion, and an average of 11,118 fW (5.31 times that of the initial forward locomotion) during turning (Figure 4A).
evidence: Calculated from simulation results shown in Figure 4A

claim: During escaping behavior, the worm produced an average power of 16,437 fW in backward locomotion, which is 7.85 times that of the initial forward locomotion.
source: During escaping behavior, the worm produced an average power of 2094 fW in the initial forward locomotion, followed by an average of 16,437 fW (7.85 times that of the initial forward locomotion) in backward locomotion, and an average of 11,118 fW (5.31 times that of the initial forward locomotion) during turning (Figure 4A).
evidence: Calculated from simulation results shown in Figure 4A

claim: During escaping behavior, the worm produced an average power of 11,118 fW during turning, which is 5.31 times that of the initial forward locomotion.
source: During escaping behavior, the worm produced an average power of 2094 fW in the initial forward locomotion, followed by an average of 16,437 fW (7.85 times that of the initial forward locomotion) in backward locomotion, and an average of 11,118 fW (5.31 times that of the initial forward locomotion) during turning (Figure 4A).
evidence: Calculated from simulation results shown in Figure 4A

claim: During escaping behavior, after turning and resuming forward locomotion, the worm produced an average power of 5480 fW, which is 2.62 times that of the initial forward locomotion.
source: After turning and resuming forward locomotion, it produced an average power of 5480 fW (2.62 times that of the initial forward locomotion).
evidence: Calculated from simulation results

claim: During delta-turn, the worm produced an average power of 3514 fW in the initial forward locomotion.
source: The worm produced an average power of 3514 fW in the initial forward locomotion, followed by an average of 11,176 fW (3.18 times that of the initial forward locomotion) in subsequent backward locomotion.
evidence: Calculated from simulation results

claim: During delta-turn, the worm produced an average power of 11,176 fW in backward locomotion, which is 3.18 times that of the initial forward locomotion.
source: The worm produced an average power of 3514 fW in the initial forward locomotion, followed by an average of 11,176 fW (3.18 times that of the initial forward locomotion) in subsequent backward locomotion.
evidence: Calculated from simulation results

claim: During delta-turn, in the relatively short duration of forward locomotion following the backward locomotion, the worm produced an average power of 17,544 fW, which is 4.99 times that of the initial forward locomotion.
source: In the relatively short duration of forward locomotion following the backward locomotion, the worm produced an average power of 17,544 fW (4.99 times that of the initial forward locomotion), and an average of 13,046 fW (3.71 times that of the initial forward locomotion) during turns (Figure 4B).
evidence: Calculated from simulation results shown in Figure 4B

claim: During delta-turn, the worm produced an average power of 13,046 fW during turns, which is 3.71 times that of the initial forward locomotion.
source: In the relatively short duration of forward locomotion following the backward locomotion, the worm produced an average power of 17,544 fW (4.99 times that of the initial forward locomotion), and an average of 13,046 fW (3.71 times that of the initial forward locomotion) during turns (Figure 4B).
evidence: Calculated from simulation results shown in Figure 4B

claim: During delta-turn, after the turn and resuming forward locomotion, the worm produced an average power of 6429 fW, which is 1.83 times that of the initial forward locomotion.
source: After the turn, when resuming forward locomotion, the worm produced an average power of 6429 fW (1.83 times that of the initial forward locomotion).
evidence: Calculated from simulation results

claim: In both escaping behavior and delta-turn, the worm consistently produced more power in the subsequent backward locomotion and turn than in the initial forward locomotion.
source: In both escaping behavior and delta-turn, the worm consistently produced more power in the subsequent backward locomotion and turn than in the initial forward locomotion.
evidence: Inferred from the power calculations for both behaviors

claim: The ElegansBot reproduced various locomotion of C. elegans including forward-backward-(omega turn)-forward locomotion constituting escaping behavior and delta-turn navigation.
source: As a result, we were able to demonstrate trajectories and kinetics of the general locomotion of C. elegans, such as crawling, swimming (Vidal-Gadea et al., 2011), omega-turn, and delta-turn (Broekmans et al., 2016).
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results with references to experimental data

claim: The trajectory obtained from ElegansBot accurately reproduces the experimental video.
source: The trajectory (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—videos 1 and 2) obtained from ElegansBot accurately reproduces the experimental video (Broekmans et al., 2016).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing simulation results with experimental videos from Broekmans et al., 2016

claim: During the omega-turn or delta-turn, the body briefly performs a deep bend, and the worm gains significant propulsion from the deep bend region to change direction.
source: Additionally, during the omega-turn or delta-turn, the body briefly performs a deep bend, and we newly discovered the mechanism that gains significant propulsion from the deep bend region to change direction using ElegansBot (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Newly discovered from simulation results shown in Figure 3C and D

claim: The only external force acting on the worm is a frictional force from a ground surface.
source: The only external force acting on the worm is a frictional force from a ground surface such as an agar plate or water.
evidence: Stated as a modeling assumption

claim: The frictional force is an anisotropic Stokes frictional force, with a magnitude proportional to the speed.
source: The frictional force is an anisotropic Stokes frictional force, with a magnitude proportional to the speed and assumed different friction coefficients in perpendicular and parallel directions (Boyle et al., 2012), which guarantees that linearity in velocity is preserved in frictional force as well (Details in 'Preservation of linearity in friction' of Appendix).
evidence: Stated as a modeling assumption with citation to Boyle et al., 2012

claim: The known crawling speed range of C. elegans matches the speed in the simulation.
source: The known crawling speed range of C. elegans (Cohen et al., 2012; Jung et al., 2016; Omura et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2012) matches the speed in our simulation.
evidence: Comparison of simulation results with cited experimental values

claim: The force dispersion pattern of the forward movement of a snake is similar to the force dispersion pattern of crawling in the ElegansBot model.
source: The force dispersion pattern of the forward movement of a snake (Hu et al., 2009) is similar to the force dispersion pattern of crawling in our model, where the body part placed diagonally in the direction of movement generates thrust.
evidence: Comparison with results from Hu et al., 2009

claim: The head and tail tracks of the simulation resemble the trace left on the agar plate by C. elegans during locomotion.
source: The head and tail tracks of our simulation resemble the trace left on the agar plate by C. elegans during locomotion (Yeon et al., 2018), providing evidence of the mechanism where C. elegans moves forward by pushing along the ground surface.
evidence: Comparison with experimental observations from Yeon et al., 2018

claim: Previous work eliminated inertia from the equations of motion, but the ElegansBot simulation includes it.
source: Previous work (Berri et al., 2009; Boyle et al., 2012) eliminated inertia from the equations of motion, but our simulation includes it, allowing calculation even in cases where inertia is significant due to low friction coefficients.
evidence: Comparison with previous work cited (Berri et al., 2009; Boyle et al., 2012)

claim: The ElegansBot simulation allows for kinetic analysis of behaviors.
source: Given that our simulation allows for kinetic analysis, it could be used to calculate the energy expended by the worm during locomotion, serving as an activity index.
evidence: Stated as a capability of the model based on its design

claim: The ElegansBot simulation only requires the body angles as input data.
source: Our simulation only requires the body angles as input data, so even if the video angle shifts and trajectory information is lost, the trajectory can be recovered from the kymogram.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the model

claim: The ElegansBot could be used to check how signals from neural network models manifest as behaviors.
source: It could be used to check how signals from neural network models manifest as behaviors which is a needed function from previous work (Sakamoto et al., 2021), and it could be used when studying compound models of neural circuits and bodies.
evidence: Stated as a potential application with reference to Sakamoto et al., 2021

claim: The ElegansBot method could be used in general for the broad utility to analyze the motion of rod-shaped animals like snakes or eels and to simulate the motion of rod-shaped robots.
source: Finally, our method could be used in general for the broad utility to analyze the motion of rod-shaped animals like snakes or eels and to simulate the motion of rod-shaped robots.
evidence: Stated as a potential application based on the generality of the model

claim: Videos of C. elegans' escaping behavior and foraging behavior were obtained from previous work.
source: Videos of C. elegans' escaping behavior and foraging behavior were obtained from previous work (Broekmans et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as the source of experimental data with citation

claim: Tierpsy Tracker was used to extract the body angles and midline from the video of C. elegans.
source: The body angles and midline were extracted using Tierpsy Tracker (Javer et al., 2018) from the original video where the worm is locomoting.
evidence: Stated as a method with citation to Javer et al., 2018

claim: WormPose was used to extract the body angles and midline of a coiled worm using a generative method.
source: WormPose trained an artificial neural network to extract the body angles and midline of a coiled worm using a generative method based on the input data.
evidence: Stated as a method with implicit reference to WormPose (Hebert et al., 2021)

claim: Python version 3.8 was used to implement the equations constituting ElegansBot.
source: Python (van Aken et al., 1995) version 3.8 was used to implement the equations constituting ElegansBot as a program.
evidence: Stated as implementation detail with citation

claim: The ElegansBot simulation of 10 s of simulation time was calculated in about 10 s of run-time on an Intel E3-1230v5 CPU.
source: This code calculated the ElegansBot simulation of 10 s of simulation time in about 10 s of run-time on an Intel E3-1230v5 CPU.
evidence: Stated as performance metric

claim: The friction coefficient values for the ground surface and the elastic and damping coefficients of C. elegans muscles were obtained from previous work.
source: The friction coefficient values for the ground surface where C. elegans crawled and swam and the elastic and damping coefficients of C. elegans muscles were obtained from previous work (Boyle et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citation to Boyle et al., 2012

claim: The changes in the direction of movement caused by turns are well replicated by ElegansBot.
source: The changes in the direction of movement caused by turns are well replicated.
evidence: Observed from simulation results

claim: The ElegansBot accurately reproduces complex behaviors like the sequence of forward-backward-turn-forward, also known as escaping behavior.
source: Moreover, the ElegansBot accurately reproduces not only the turns but also complex behaviors like the sequence of forward-backward-turn-forward, also known as escaping behavior.
evidence: Demonstrated through simulation results

claim: C. elegans performs various behaviors such as locomotion, sleeping, reproduction, and hunting.
source: With only a few hundred neurons, Caenorhabditis Elegans (C. elegans) perform various behaviors such as locomotion, sleeping, reproduction, and hunting (Hall and Altun, 2008).
evidence: Stated with citation to Hall and Altun, 2008

claim: C. elegans is a cost-efficient and widely used model in neuronal research.
source: C. elegans is a cost-efficient and widely used model in neuronal research.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The small body size and minimal nutritional requirements of C. elegans contribute to its cost efficiency.
source: Its small body size and minimal nutritional requirements contribute to its cost efficiency.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Offspring of C. elegans mostly share the same genotype as the parent due to its hermaphroditic nature.
source: Moreover, due to the hermaphroditic nature of C. elegans, offspring mostly share the same genotype as the parent, which simplifies the multiplication of the worm population for research purposes (Hall and Altun, 2008).
evidence: Stated with citation to Hall and Altun, 2008

claim: A worm has difficulties in forward and backward locomotion if it does not feel the difference in frictional forces from its surroundings.
source: Even if a worm has a sinusoidal modulation generated inside it, it has difficulties in forward and backward locomotion if it does not feel the difference in frictional forces from its surroundings.
evidence: Stated as a principle of locomotion

claim: Mechanical simulators of rod-shaped animals have been used in various studies.
source: Mechanical simulators of rod-shaped animals such as C. elegans (Boyle et al., 2012; Niebur and Erdös, 1991), fish (Ekeberg, 1993), and snakes Hu et al., 2009 have been used in various studies.
evidence: Stated with citations to multiple studies

claim: These simulators demonstrate how the activities of muscle cells are represented as behavioral phenotypes.
source: These simulators demonstrate how the activities of muscle cells are represented as behavioral phenotypes, which are determined by signals from a neuronal circuit simulator (Boyle et al., 2012; Ekeberg, 1993; Niebur and Erdös, 1991).
evidence: Stated with citations to Boyle et al., 2012; Ekeberg, 1993; Niebur and Erdös, 1991

claim: To the authors' best knowledge, there was no kinetic model that reproduces complex locomotion behavior of C. elegans including all various modes of locomotion from experimental observations.
source: Even though there were studies on kinematic simulation of rod-shaped animals (Boyle et al., 2012; Ekeberg, 1993; Hu et al., 2009), to our best knowledge, there was no kinetic model that reproduces complex locomotion behavior of C. elegans, which includes all of the various modes of locomotion of C. elegans such as forward locomotion, backward locomotion, and turn from experimental observations.
evidence: Stated as a gap in the literature with citations to previous work

claim: The authors built a Newtonian-mechanics two-dimensional rigid body chain model of C. elegans to reproduce its locomotion.
source: We built a Newtonian-mechanics two-dimensional rigid body chain model of C. elegans to reproduce its locomotion.
evidence: Stated as the main contribution of the work

claim: The model includes a chain of multiple rod rigid bodies, a damped torsional spring between the rigid bodies, and a control angle.
source: The model includes a chain of multiple rod rigid bodies, a damped torsional spring between the rigid bodies, and a control angle, which is the dynamic baseline angle from the value of the kymogram of a physical experiment.
evidence: Stated as a description of the model

claim: The authors formulated Newtonian equations of translational and rotational motion of the rigid body model and computed the numerical solution using the semi-implicit Euler method.
source: We formulated Newtonian equations of translational and rotational motion of the rigid body model and computed the numerical solution of the equations by numerical integration using the semi-implicit Euler method.
evidence: Stated as the methodology

claim: The authors were able to demonstrate trajectories and kinetics of general locomotion of C. elegans, such as crawling, swimming, omega-turn, and delta-turn.
source: As a result, we were able to demonstrate trajectories and kinetics of the general locomotion of C. elegans, such as crawling, swimming (Vidal-Gadea et al., 2011), omega-turn, and delta-turn (Broekmans et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as the results with citations to experimental data
